item.title: Kyoto Tower: The City's Only Skyscraper View — Guide
item.description: Kyoto Tower, completed in 1964 and standing 131 metres directly across from Kyoto Station, is the tallest structure in a city that otherwise keeps deliberately low to protect its skyline. Its slender white form, said to evoke a lighthouse or a candle, is a divisive landmark but an unbeatable viewpoint: because Kyoto has no other tall buildings, the observation deck at 100 metres gives a genuinely uninterrupted 360-degree panorama over the whole basin, the grid of the old city, the scattered pagodas and temple roofs, and the mountains that ring it on three sides.

item.title: Sapporo Clock Tower — Guide
item.description: The Sapporo Clock Tower (Tokeidai) is one of the city’s most famous and beloved symbols, a charming wooden building in the American colonial style that dates from Hokkaido’s pioneer development era. Built in 1878 as a drill hall for the Sapporo Agricultural College (the forerunner of Hokkaido University), it was fitted with its distinctive tower clock in 1881 — a mechanism imported from Boston that still keeps time today, making it one of the oldest working tower clocks in Japan.

item.title: Tokyo Tower — Guide
item.description: Tokyo Tower, standing 333 metres tall in the Shiba-koen district, is one of the city’s most beloved and enduring symbols. Painted in distinctive orange and white and inspired by the Eiffel Tower, it was completed in 1958 as a broadcasting tower and quickly became an icon of post-war Tokyo’s rebirth. Though now surpassed in height by the Skytree, Tokyo Tower retains a special nostalgic, retro charm. Two observation decks — the Main Deck at 150 m and the higher Top Deck at 250 m — offer sweeping panoramic views over the city, taking in landmarks, Tokyo Bay and, on clear days, Mount Fuji, and the views are especially romantic after dark when the city lights up.

item.title: Iwate Bank Red Brick Building: Morioka's Meiji Landmark — Guide
item.description: The Iwate Bank Red Brick Building is one of Morioka’s best-loved landmarks — a handsome 1911 former bank designed by Kingo Tatsuno, architect of Tokyo Station, and his partner. Its red brick and white stone facade anchors the historic city centre, and the beautifully restored interior is open to visitors. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Morioka, Iwate Hours ~10:00–16:30 (closed Tue) Admission Around ¥300 (interior) Time needed About 40 min Best time Year-round What to See The red brick and white stone Meiji facade (1911).
